Culminate.fullDefinition: To culminate is to arrive at the high point or conclusion of a process.

Culpable.example: He was found culpable for the accident.
Culpable.fullDefinition: Culpable refers to being legally or morally responsible for wrongdoing.

Cumbersome.example: The cumbersome approval process discouraged small businesses from applying.
Cumbersome.fullDefinition: Something cumbersome is awkward to handle because of its size, weight, or complexity.

Cumulative.example: The cumulative impact of minor regulations proved greater than any single law.
Cumulative.fullDefinition: A cumulative effect builds up gradually as each new increment adds to what came before.

Curmudgeon.example: The columnist cultivated a reputation as a lovable curmudgeon who disliked all new technology.
Curmudgeon.fullDefinition: A curmudgeon is someone, often older, who is habitually grumpy and resistant to change.

Cursory.example: Even a cursory reading of the contract reveals several contradictions.
Cursory.fullDefinition: A cursory examination is done quickly, without attention to detail.

Curtail.example: Budget cuts will curtail many planned projects.
Curtail.fullDefinition: To curtail is to cut short, diminish, or impose limits on something.

Cynosure.example: The restored cathedral became the cynosure of the city's tourist trade.
Cynosure.fullDefinition: A cynosure is a person or thing that attracts everyone's admiration or interest.

Daunt.example: The sheer volume of legal documents would daunt any newcomer.
Daunt.fullDefinition: To daunt is to overawe, intimidate, or dishearten someone so that their confidence or resolve weakens in the face of a task or challenge.

Dearth.example: There was a dearth of affordable housing.
Dearth.fullDefinition: Dearth indicates an insufficient supply or shortage of something needed.

Debacle.example: The product launch was a debacle, with servers crashing within minutes.
Debacle.fullDefinition: A debacle is an abrupt, disastrous collapse or fiasco that lays plans or reputations to ruin in a very public way.

Debase.definition: to lower in quality or dignity.
Debase.example: Critics argued that the studio had debased a subtle novel into a string of predictable chase scenes.
Debase.fullDefinition: To debase something is to reduce its value, purity, or moral standing, as when a currency is diluted with cheaper metal or an ideal is cheapened by misuse.

Debunk.example: The historian spent a decade debunking the legend that the bridge had been designed by a single genius.
Debunk.fullDefinition: To debunk is to show that a widely held claim, myth, or theory is unfounded, usually by presenting contrary evidence.

Decorum.example: She spoke with perfect decorum, even when provoked.
Decorum.fullDefinition: Decorum is dignified, socially appropriate conduct in speech, dress, and manner that conforms to accepted standards of good taste.

Decry.example: Labor leaders decried the new policy as a quiet erosion of hard-won protections.
Decry.fullDefinition: To decry is to criticize something in public as wrong, harmful, or worthless, often in order to rally others against it.

Default.definition: failure to act; a standard option.
Default.example: If you don't choose a ringtone, the phone reverts to its default setting.
Default.fullDefinition: Default can mean (a) the preset or automatic choice applied when no alternative is selected, or (b) the failure to meet an obligation, perform a duty, or pay a debt.

Deference.example: Out of deference to her expertise, the team let Dr. Rao lead the discussion.
Deference.fullDefinition: Deference is courteous regard for another’s judgment, rank, or wishes, shown by yielding one’s own preferences in respectful acknowledgment.

Deferential.example: He spoke in deferential tones to the senior judge.
Deferential.fullDefinition: Deferential attitudes convey honor or esteem by acknowledging another’s authority or experience.

Deft.example: With a few deft revisions, the editor turned a meandering draft into a taut argument.
Deft.fullDefinition: Deft describes movements or handling that are quick, precise, and assured, whether in physical tasks or in delicate negotiations.

Defunct.example: The once-famous chain is now defunct, its stores long boarded up.
Defunct.fullDefinition: Defunct describes something—such as an institution, practice, or mechanism—that has ceased to operate, exist, or hold legal force.

Deign.example: The celebrated architect rarely deigned to answer questions from junior staff.
Deign.fullDefinition: To deign is to agree to do something one considers beneath one's dignity; the word usually implies arrogance in the person doing it.

Deleterious.example: Researchers documented the deleterious effects of chronic noise on children's ability to concentrate.
Deleterious.fullDefinition: Deleterious describes substances, habits, or policies that cause harm, often in ways that are not immediately obvious.

Delineate.example: The architect used bright tape to delineate each room's dimensions on the floor.
Delineate.fullDefinition: To delineate is to trace or depict the exact boundaries, details, or characteristics of something with sharp, systematic clarity.

Demagogue.definition: a leader who exploits popular prejudice.
Demagogue.example: The essay traces how a provincial demagogue rose to national prominence by blaming every hardship on outsiders.
Demagogue.fullDefinition: A demagogue is a political figure who gains power by appealing to the fears, resentments, and emotions of the crowd rather than to reasoned argument.

Demur.example: He did not demur when offered the leadership role, accepting immediately.
Demur.fullDefinition: To demur is to voice hesitation, reservations, or polite objections to a proposal, statement, or course of action.

Demure.example: Her demure public persona concealed a fiercely competitive streak in the boardroom.
Demure.fullDefinition: Demure describes a person, or their manner or dress, that is quiet, restrained, and modest, sometimes to the point of seeming affected.

Denigrate.example: It's unprofessional to denigrate a colleague's ideas in public.
Denigrate.fullDefinition: To denigrate is to criticize in a way that unfairly diminishes the value, character, or reputation of a person or thing.

Denouement.definition: the final resolution of a story.
Denouement.example: The novel’s denouement tied up all loose plot threads.
Denouement.fullDefinition: Denouement is the part of a narrative in which the strands of the plot are drawn together and matters are explained.

Deplore.definition: to regret and strongly disapprove of.
Deplore.example: The commission deplored the conditions in the detention centers but stopped short of recommending closure.
Deplore.fullDefinition: To deplore something is to consider it deeply regrettable and morally wrong, and usually to say so.

Depravity.example: The novel's villain is a figure of such depravity that some reviewers found him implausible.
Depravity.fullDefinition: Depravity is a state of profound moral decay in which a person or society has abandoned ordinary standards of decency.

Deprecate.example: The senator deprecated the rush to judgment, urging colleagues to await the full report.
Deprecate.fullDefinition: To deprecate is to voice disapproval of something, often gently; in self-deprecating remarks, speakers play down their own achievements.

Deride.example: Anonymous trolls deride every new policy, no matter how sensible.
Deride.fullDefinition: To deride is to subject someone or something to scornful laughter, sneers, or contemptuous ridicule.

Derision.example: Her proposal was met with derision from the skeptics.
Derision.fullDefinition: Derision is the act of treating someone or something with scornful ridicule.

Derivative.example: Critics complained that the film felt derivative of better-known classics.
Derivative.fullDefinition: Derivative refers to work or ideas that heavily borrow from existing sources, displaying little or no unique creativity or innovation.

Derogatory.example: The review was less a critique than a series of derogatory comments about the author's background.
Derogatory.fullDefinition: Derogatory remarks or terms show disrespect for someone or something and are meant to diminish their standing.

Descry.definition: to catch sight of; to discover.
Descry.example: From the hilltop, they descried smoke rising in the valley.
Descry.fullDefinition: To descry is to perceive or detect something that is difficult to see by looking carefully.

Desecrate.example: Vandals desecrated the memorial on the eve of the anniversary, provoking outrage across the city.
Desecrate.fullDefinition: To desecrate is to treat a holy or deeply respected place or object with violent disrespect.

Desiccate.example: Left in the sun, the oranges began to desiccate and lose flavor.
Desiccate.fullDefinition: Desiccate means to remove virtually all moisture from something, leaving it thoroughly dried; figuratively, it can mean to drain vitality or interest.

Despondent.example: After the third rejected grant proposal, the team grew despondent about the project's future.
Despondent.fullDefinition: Despondent describes someone who has lost heart and sees little prospect that things will improve.

Despot.definition: a ruler with absolute, often cruel, power.
Despot.example: The chronicle portrays the king not as a reformer but as a despot who silenced every rival.
Despot.fullDefinition: A despot is a ruler who governs with unchecked authority and often uses it oppressively.

Desuetude.definition: a state of disuse or inactivity.
Desuetude.example: Many ancient customs fell into desuetude over centuries.
Desuetude.fullDefinition: Desuetude denotes a condition in which something is no longer practiced or used; disuse.

Desultory.example: Their desultory conversation skipped from sports to politics to cooking without depth.
Desultory.fullDefinition: Desultory describes activity or discourse that moves haphazardly from one subject to another, showing scant consistency or enthusiasm.

Deterrent.example: Visible security cameras serve as a deterrent to shoplifters.
Deterrent.fullDefinition: A deterrent is any factor—punishment, obstacle, or fear—that discourages or restrains someone from undertaking a particular action.

Diaphanous.example: She wore a diaphanous gown that fluttered in the breeze.
Diaphanous.fullDefinition: Diaphanous describes fabric or material so fine that it allows light to pass through.

Diatribe.example: The editorial was a scathing diatribe against government corruption.
Diatribe.fullDefinition: A diatribe is an extended, vehement denunciation or tirade directed at a person, policy, or idea.

Dichotomy.example: The play explores the dichotomy between duty and personal desire.
Dichotomy.fullDefinition: A dichotomy is a clear, often mutually exclusive division or contrast between two opposed groups, concepts, or classifications.

Dictum.example: The architect's famous dictum that form follows function shaped a generation of buildings.
Dictum.fullDefinition: A dictum is a formal statement of opinion or principle, often from an acknowledged authority, that others come to treat as a rule.

Didactic.example: Aesop’s fables are didactic, each ending with a moral lesson.
Didactic.fullDefinition: Didactic works or methods aim primarily to instruct or moralize, sometimes at the expense of entertainment or subtlety.

Die.example: Many flowers die without sufficient water.
Die.fullDefinition: To die is to stop living or functioning; to pass from life to death.

Diffidence.example: Her diffidence in speaking up made people underestimate her knowledge.
Diffidence.fullDefinition: Diffidence is modesty or timidity arising from self-doubt, leading to reluctance in asserting one’s ideas or abilities.

Diffuse.example: Sunlight became diffuse behind the thick fog.
Diffuse.fullDefinition: As an adjective, diffuse means scattered and lacking focus or brevity; as a verb, it means to disperse something widely in many directions.

Digression.definition: a departure from the main topic.
Digression.example: After a brief digression about his dog, the lecturer returned to quantum theory.
Digression.fullDefinition: A digression is a temporary sidetrack in speech or writing that strays from the central argument or narrative.

Dilapidated.example: The foundation purchased a dilapidated mill and restored it as a regional museum.
Dilapidated.fullDefinition: Dilapidated describes a building or object that has decayed through age, neglect, or lack of upkeep.

Dilatory.example: The defense's dilatory motions pushed the trial back by nearly a year.
Dilatory.fullDefinition: Dilatory describes a person or tactic that is slow to act, or that is deliberately meant to stall progress.

Dilettante.example: He was a dilettante in literature, never taking it seriously.
Dilettante.fullDefinition: Dilettante describes someone who engages in an art or field lightly without real commitment or mastery.

Diligent.example: Only a diligent review of the archival records revealed the discrepancy in the dates.
Diligent.fullDefinition: Diligent describes a person or effort marked by steady, conscientious attention to a task.

Dirge.example: A slow dirge echoed through the hall as mourners filed past the casket.
Dirge.fullDefinition: A dirge is a solemn, mournful musical composition or chant performed as part of funeral rites to express grief for the dead.

Disabuse.example: The mentor worked to disabuse him of the notion that success comes easily.
Disabuse.fullDefinition: To disabuse is to rid someone of mistaken ideas or false beliefs by presenting accurate information.

Disaffected.example: The campaign courted disaffected voters who felt that neither party represented them.
Disaffected.fullDefinition: Disaffected describes people who have become dissatisfied with and estranged from an authority, party, or cause they once supported.

Disavow.example: The scientist later disavowed her early findings after repeated attempts to replicate them failed.
Disavow.fullDefinition: To disavow is to refuse to acknowledge or accept responsibility for something, such as a statement, a group, or a past belief.

Discerning.example: With a discerning eye, she selected the ripest peaches at the market.
Discerning.fullDefinition: Discerning denotes the ability to perceive fine distinctions and exercise keen, insightful judgment.

Disconcert.example: The witness was visibly disconcerted by the prosecutor's abrupt change of subject.
Disconcert.fullDefinition: To disconcert someone is to disturb their composure, leaving them uneasy or confused.

Discordant.example: The band was out of tune, producing a discordant jumble of sounds.
Discordant.fullDefinition: Discordant can mean (a) producing sounds that clash harshly, or (b) marked by disagreement and lack of harmony between people or ideas.

Discredit.example: One scandal was enough to discredit the entire administration.
Discredit.fullDefinition: To discredit is to undermine trust or confidence in someone or something, causing others to regard it as unreliable or untrue.

Discrepancy.example: An accountant noticed a discrepancy between the invoices and the payments.
Discrepancy.fullDefinition: A discrepancy is a lack of agreement or correspondence between facts, figures, or accounts that should match.

Discrete.example: The course is divided into discrete modules that can be studied separately.
Discrete.fullDefinition: Discrete refers to elements that are individually separate and unconnected, standing apart as self-contained units rather than forming a continuous whole.

Discretion.example: Use discretion when sharing sensitive information.
Discretion.fullDefinition: Discretion is the ability to make responsible decisions and maintain confidentiality or tact.

Discursive.example: The memoir is discursive, wandering from childhood anecdotes to reflections on economic theory.
Discursive.fullDefinition: Discursive writing or speech moves freely from subject to subject; in philosophy, the word can also mean proceeding by reasoned argument rather than intuition.

Disdain.example: The critic made no attempt to hide his disdain for commercial fiction.
Disdain.fullDefinition: Disdain is the feeling that someone or something is beneath one's notice or respect; as a verb, it means to reject with such scorn.

Disgruntled.example: The disgruntled employees voiced their complaints at the meeting.
Disgruntled.fullDefinition: Disgruntled refers to someone who is discontented and resentful about a situation.

Disingenuous.example: His sudden show of concern felt disingenuous to those who knew him.
Disingenuous.fullDefinition: Disingenuous describes behavior that is not fully honest or straightforward, often masking true motives behind a pose of innocence or candor.

Disinterested.example: A disinterested mediator can help both sides reach an agreement.
Disinterested.fullDefinition: Disinterested denotes freedom from personal stake or prejudice, enabling objective judgment based solely on facts or fairness.

Disjointed.example: The report felt disjointed, with ideas presented in no logical order.
Disjointed.fullDefinition: Disjointed describes speech, writing, or parts that are disconnected and incoherent, failing to form a smooth or logical whole.

Dismiss.definition: to reject or put away from consideration.
Dismiss.example: The judge moved to dismiss the case for lack of evidence.
Dismiss.fullDefinition: To dismiss is to refuse to accept or entertain something—such as an idea, complaint, or legal action—deeming it unworthy of further attention.

Disparage.example: He tended to disparage any suggestion that wasn't his own.
Disparage.fullDefinition: To disparage is to belittle or speak of something in a way that diminishes its value, reputation, or credibility.

Disparate.example: The panel brought together disparate viewpoints from science, art, and business.
Disparate.fullDefinition: Disparate describes items or ideas so unlike in kind or quality that direct comparison is difficult or impossible.

Dispassionate.example: A dispassionate judge must weigh evidence objectively.
Dispassionate.fullDefinition: Dispassionate describes an approach devoid of strong emotion, ensuring fairness and objectivity.

Dispel.definition: to drive away a belief or feeling.
Dispel.example: The new data did little to dispel concerns about the drug's long-term safety.
Dispel.fullDefinition: To dispel is to make a doubt, fear, or misconception disappear, often by offering clear evidence against it.

Disquiet.example: The minister's vague assurances only deepened public disquiet over the water supply.
Disquiet.fullDefinition: Disquiet is a state of anxiety or worry, often about something not yet fully understood.

Dissemble.example: Knowing the negotiations were televised, she had to dissemble her frustration.
Dissemble.fullDefinition: To dissemble is to conceal real intentions, emotions, or facts under a false appearance, often for strategic advantage.

Disseminate.example: Public health officials disseminate information about vaccines through social media.
Disseminate.fullDefinition: Disseminate means to distribute something—especially knowledge, news, or data—widely so it reaches many people or places.

Dissident.example: Several dissidents were exiled after publishing essays critical of the regime.
Dissident.fullDefinition: A dissident is a person who openly challenges the established doctrine or authority, especially that of a state or institution.

Dissipate.example: The early enthusiasm for the reform dissipated once its costs became clear.
Dissipate.fullDefinition: To dissipate is to disperse or vanish gradually, or to waste resources, energy, or money foolishly.

Dissolution.definition: the breaking up or dissolving of something.
Dissolution.example: Shareholders voted for the company's dissolution after years of losses.
Dissolution.fullDefinition: Dissolution is the formal disintegration or termination of an organization, partnership, or legal entity, ending its existence or functions.

Dissonance.definition: lack of harmony or agreement in sound.
Dissonance.example: The composer used intentional dissonance to create tension in the piece.
Dissonance.fullDefinition: Dissonance literally refers to clashing, unresolved musical tones; figuratively, it denotes a state of conflict or inconsistency among ideas, beliefs, or perceptions.

Dissuade.definition: to talk someone out of an action.
Dissuade.example: Her advisers tried to dissuade her from publishing the letters before the election.
Dissuade.fullDefinition: To dissuade is to persuade a person not to take a particular course of action.

Distend.example: After the feast, his stomach began to distend uncomfortably.
Distend.fullDefinition: To distend is to stretch outward and enlarge, often from internal pressure, causing swelling or bloating.

Distill.definition: to purify or extract the essence.
Distill.example: The editor asked her to distill the twenty-page report into a one-page brief.
Distill.fullDefinition: Distill means to remove impurities through vaporization and condensation—or, figuratively, to refine complex material down to its most essential elements.

Diverge.example: Opinions began to diverge as the discussion moved to policy details.
Diverge.fullDefinition: To diverge is to separate from a common point, path, or opinion, moving or developing in distinct directions.

Divergent.example: The two species followed divergent evolutionary paths.
Divergent.fullDefinition: Divergent ideas, lines, or paths move apart from a common point, emphasizing deviation.

Divest.example: Under pressure, the university agreed to divest from fossil-fuel companies.
Divest.fullDefinition: To divest is to rid oneself of property, rights, or investments—or to deprive another entity of possession or status.

Divisive.example: Few topics proved as divisive within the council as the proposed zoning changes.
Divisive.fullDefinition: Divisive describes issues, figures, or actions that split people into opposing camps.

Docile.example: Colonial administrators mistakenly assumed that the population would remain docile under the new taxes.
Docile.fullDefinition: Docile describes a person or animal that is quiet and readily accepts control or instruction.

Doctrinaire.example: Her doctrinaire approach to economics left little room for the exceptions that real markets produce.
Doctrinaire.fullDefinition: Doctrinaire describes someone who insists on applying a doctrine or theory without regard to practical circumstances.

Dogged.example: Only the reporter's dogged investigation brought the fraud to light.
Dogged.fullDefinition: Dogged describes determination that refuses to give up despite difficulty or slow progress.

Dogmatic.example: His dogmatic insistence on doing things ‘the right way’ stifled creativity.
Dogmatic.fullDefinition: Dogmatic describes asserting principles as incontrovertibly true, allowing no questioning or dissent, often with arrogant rigidity.

Dormant.example: The volcano had been dormant for centuries before erupting unexpectedly.
Dormant.fullDefinition: Dormant means temporarily inactive or in a state of suspended function, yet capable of being reawakened or reactivated.

Dour.example: The dour headmaster rarely smiled, even at graduation.
Dour.fullDefinition: Dour describes a person, expression, or manner that is severe, humorless, and unfriendly.

Draconian.example: Critics called the draconian sentences for minor offenses a betrayal of the justice system's aims.
Draconian.fullDefinition: Draconian describes laws, rules, or penalties that are extremely severe, often out of proportion to the offense.

Droll.example: His droll commentary on committee procedure made the dry minutes surprisingly readable.
Droll.fullDefinition: Droll describes humor that is quiet, whimsical, and understated, provoking a smile more often than laughter.

Dubious.example: The study's conclusions rest on the dubious assumption that survey respondents answered honestly.
Dubious.fullDefinition: Dubious describes something that invites suspicion or uncertainty, or a person who feels hesitant about it.

Dupe.definition: to trick or deceive; a victim of deception.
Dupe.example: A fake invoice managed to dupe the company into paying thousands.
Dupe.fullDefinition: As a verb, dupe means to deceive or cheat; as a noun, it denotes someone who has been misled or taken advantage of.

Duplicity.example: The diplomat's duplicity came to light when the two governments compared the contradictory assurances he had given each.
Duplicity.fullDefinition: Duplicity is the practice of deceiving others by speaking or acting in two contradictory ways.

Earnest.example: Despite its earnest tone, the pamphlet persuaded few readers.
Earnest.fullDefinition: Earnest describes a person or effort that is wholehearted and serious in intention, sometimes to the point of lacking humor.

Ebullient.definition: full of high spirits; cheerful and energetic.
Ebullient.example: Her ebullient laugh filled the room and instantly lifted everyone’s mood.
Ebullient.fullDefinition: Ebullient characterizes overflowing enthusiasm, vivacity, and cheerful energy that bubbles up like boiling liquid.

Eccentric.example: His eccentric wardrobe choices always turned heads at the office.
Eccentric.fullDefinition: Eccentric refers to behavior, ideas, or appearance that deviates noticeably from accepted norms, often in a quirky or whimsical way.

Eclectic.example: The restaurant’s eclectic menu offered sushi, tacos, and Italian gelato on the same page.
Eclectic.fullDefinition: Eclectic describes taste or style that draws from a broad, diverse range of ideas, traditions, or influences rather than adhering to a single approach.

Ecstatic.example: She was ecstatic upon receiving the award.
Ecstatic.fullDefinition: Ecstatic describes a feeling or expression of intense, often overwhelming, happiness or excitement.

Edify.example: Victorian novelists often sought to edify their readers as much as to entertain them.
Edify.fullDefinition: To edify is to teach someone in a way that improves their mind or character.

Efface.example: Centuries of wind and rain had effaced the inscriptions on the tomb.
Efface.fullDefinition: To efface is to wipe out or wear away a mark or memory; to efface oneself is to keep deliberately out of notice.

Effete.example: The revolutionaries mocked the aristocracy as effete and incapable of governing.
Effete.fullDefinition: Effete describes a person or culture that has become feeble and self-indulgent, lacking its former vigor.

Efficacy.example: Clinical trials proved the vaccine’s efficacy in preventing infection.
Efficacy.fullDefinition: Efficacy is the capacity of an intervention, drug, or method to achieve its intended or desired effect under ideal conditions.

Effrontery.example: He had the effrontery to arrive late and then criticize everyone else’s punctuality.
Effrontery.fullDefinition: Effrontery denotes brazen, impudent behavior that ignores normal boundaries of respect or courtesy.

Effusive.example: The normally reserved critic was effusive in her praise of the debut album.
Effusive.fullDefinition: Effusive describes praise, gratitude, or emotion that pours out lavishly, sometimes excessively.

Egalitarian.example: The commune's egalitarian ideals were tested when some members began contributing far less than others.
Egalitarian.fullDefinition: Egalitarian describes a belief, society, or practice founded on the principle that all people deserve equal rights and opportunities.

Egregious.example: The report cited several egregious errors in the agency's handling of the evidence.
Egregious.fullDefinition: Egregious describes an error, offense, or failure so extreme that it stands out from ordinary mistakes.

Elegy.example: She wrote an elegy for her grandmother, weaving memories into tender verse.
Elegy.fullDefinition: An elegy is a reflective, plaintive literary or musical work lamenting the death of an individual or the passing of something valued.

Elicit.example: Skilled interviewers use open-ended questions to elicit detailed answers.
Elicit.fullDefinition: To elicit is to bring forth or evoke information, emotions, or reactions through skillful inquiry or stimulation.

Elliptical.example: The poet's elliptical style rewards patient readers but frustrates casual ones.
Elliptical.fullDefinition: Elliptical describes speech or writing that leaves so much unsaid that its meaning is hard to grasp; it can also mean oval in shape.

Eloquent.example: Her eloquent closing argument swayed the jury to acquit.
Eloquent.fullDefinition: Eloquent speech or writing conveys ideas with fluency, grace, and emotional force, moving audiences through vivid language and compelling structure.

Elucidate.example: The second chapter elucidates the theory that the first merely sketches.
Elucidate.fullDefinition: To elucidate is to explain something complicated or obscure so that it becomes understandable.

Elusive.definition: difficult to catch or pin down.
Elusive.example: A cure for the disease has proved elusive despite decades of research.
Elusive.fullDefinition: Elusive describes something that evades capture, definition, or memory.

Embellish.example: He loves to embellish his stories with dramatic details that never happened.
Embellish.fullDefinition: Embellish means to beautify by adding ornamental details—or to enhance a story with imaginative, sometimes exaggerated, additions.

Embroil.example: The museum became embroiled in a legal dispute over the provenance of its antiquities.
Embroil.fullDefinition: To embroil is to involve a person or group deeply in an argument, conflict, or difficult situation.

Eminence.example: The scientist’s eminence in the field of genetics was acknowledged worldwide.
Eminence.fullDefinition: Eminence refers to a position of high distinction, honor, or renown, especially within a particular profession or sphere of activity.

Emollient.example: The lotion had an emollient effect on her skin.
Emollient.fullDefinition: Emollient describes substances or actions that soften and soothe, especially skin.

Empirical.example: The theory sounded plausible, but it needed empirical data to back it up.
Empirical.fullDefinition: Empirical applies to knowledge, methods, or conclusions that rely on direct observation, measurement, or experimentation rather than on theory, speculation, or pure logic.

Emulate.definition: to imitate in order to equal or excel.
Emulate.example: Young artists often emulate Picasso’s bold colors before finding their own style.
Emulate.fullDefinition: To emulate is to strive to match or surpass a person or model by intentional imitation of their qualities, techniques, or achievements.

Encomium.definition: a formal expression of high praise.
Encomium.example: The committee delivered an encomium to the retiring professor.
Encomium.fullDefinition: An encomium is a laudatory speech or piece of writing that publicly praises someone or something.

Encroach.example: Suburban development continues to encroach on the remaining wetlands.
Encroach.fullDefinition: To encroach is to advance steadily into territory, rights, or time that belongs to someone else.

Encumber.definition: to weigh down with a burden.
Encumber.example: The startup was encumbered by loans it had taken on during its first year.
Encumber.fullDefinition: To encumber is to load with a burden, such as debt or obligation, that restricts movement or freedom of action.

Endemic.definition: native or restricted to a region.
Endemic.example: Malaria is endemic to some tropical regions but almost unheard-of here.
Endemic.fullDefinition: Endemic denotes a disease, species, or practice that is consistently present or confined to a particular geographic area or population.

Enervate.example: The sweltering heat enervated the runners before the race even began.
Enervate.fullDefinition: To enervate is to sap physical, mental, or moral strength, leaving someone languid, weary, or less able to function.

Engender.example: Transparent policies engender trust between management and staff.
Engender.fullDefinition: Engender means to bring into existence, give rise to, or foster a feeling, condition, or situation.

Enhance.example: A sprinkle of sea salt can enhance the sweetness of dark chocolate.
Enhance.fullDefinition: Enhance is to heighten, intensify, or augment the quality, attractiveness, or effectiveness of something already in place.

Enigmatic.example: The scientist’s enigmatic smile suggested he knew more than he was saying.
Enigmatic.fullDefinition: Enigmatic describes persons, statements, or phenomena that are puzzling, cryptic, or shrouded in ambiguity, inviting speculation.

Enmity.example: The enmity between the two families outlasted the dispute that had caused it.
Enmity.fullDefinition: Enmity is a state of active, often long-standing hostility between people or groups.

Ennui.example: She felt a deep ennui during the long, uneventful summer.
Ennui.fullDefinition: Ennui is a feeling of weariness and dissatisfaction arising from lack of occupation or excitement.

Enormity.example: Only years later did the public grasp the enormity of the crimes committed in the camps.
Enormity.fullDefinition: Enormity refers to the extreme seriousness or monstrousness of a wrong; careful writers distinguish it from mere enormousness.

Ensconce.example: Ensconced in a corner of the library, the scholar worked undisturbed for hours.
Ensconce.fullDefinition: To ensconce is to establish oneself or something firmly in a comfortable, safe, or hidden position.

Enthrall.example: The lecturer enthralled the audience with her account of the expedition.
Enthrall.fullDefinition: To enthrall is to hold someone's attention so fully that they are charmed or spellbound.

Entrenched.definition: firmly established and hard to change.
Entrenched.fullDefinition: Entrenched refers to attitudes, practices, or structures that are deeply rooted and resistant to alteration.

Enumerate.example: The treaty enumerates the specific powers granted to each signatory.
Enumerate.fullDefinition: To enumerate is to name items individually, as in a list, or to count them.

Ephemeral.example: Morning fog is beautiful but ephemeral, vanishing as soon as the sun appears.
Ephemeral.fullDefinition: Ephemeral denotes things that exist or last only for a brief, transitory period before disappearing.

Epicure.definition: a connoisseur of fine food and drink.
Epicure.example: Even a demanding epicure would have found little to criticize in the chef's tasting menu.
Epicure.fullDefinition: An epicure is a person with refined, discriminating taste, especially in food and wine.

Epithet.example: Later chroniclers saddled King Ethelred with an unflattering epithet, the Unready, that has long outlived his reign.
Epithet.fullDefinition: An epithet is a word or phrase attached to a name to characterize the person; in modern usage, it often means an abusive term.

Epitome.definition: the embodiment of a type or quality.
Epitome.example: The estate was the epitome of Georgian elegance.
Epitome.fullDefinition: The epitome of something is a person or thing that represents it so completely that it serves as its model.

Equanimity.example: She handled the hostile questions with remarkable equanimity.
Equanimity.fullDefinition: Equanimity is evenness of mind and composure maintained under tension, shock, or adversity.

Equitable.example: They proposed an equitable distribution of resources between departments.
Equitable.fullDefinition: Equitable applies to decisions, systems, or treatments grounded in justice and unbiased balance, ensuring all parties receive their rightful share or consideration.

Equivocate.example: Asked about higher taxes, the governor chose to equivocate instead of saying yes or no.
Equivocate.fullDefinition: To equivocate is to use intentionally vague or evasive language so as to conceal the truth or avoid committing oneself.

Erratic.example: The patient's erratic heart rhythm alarmed the attending physician.
Erratic.fullDefinition: Erratic describes movement, behavior, or performance that follows no steady pattern.

Erroneous.example: The report was withdrawn after several erroneous statistics were discovered.
Erroneous.fullDefinition: Erroneous refers to beliefs, statements, or data that are factually wrong or based on false assumptions.

Ersatz.example: Wartime shortages forced households to brew an ersatz coffee from roasted chicory.
Ersatz.fullDefinition: Ersatz describes something made or used as a substitute, usually one that is artificial and of lower quality than the original.

Erstwhile.example: The senator found herself debating an erstwhile ally.
Erstwhile.fullDefinition: Erstwhile describes someone or something that once held a role or status but no longer does.

Erudite.example: The erudite professor could quote obscure Latin texts from memory.
Erudite.fullDefinition: Erudite characterizes deep, wide-ranging learning acquired through extensive reading and study.

Eschew.definition: to deliberately avoid or abstain from.
Eschew.example: She eschewed social media during exam week to focus on studying.
Eschew.fullDefinition: To eschew is to intentionally refrain from using, engaging in, or enjoying something considered undesirable.

Esoteric.example: Quantum-field theory remains esoteric to most laypeople.
Esoteric.fullDefinition: Esoteric refers to knowledge, doctrines, or references intended for or accessible only to a small, specialized group with the requisite background.

Essay.definition: a short written composition on a topic.
Essay.example: She submitted her essay on climate change.
Essay.fullDefinition: An essay is a brief piece of writing that explores or argues a specific theme or idea.

Estimable.example: The prize honored an estimable career in public health.
Estimable.fullDefinition: Estimable describes a person or achievement worthy of admiration and high regard.

Estranged.example: The biography explores the author's fraught relationship with his estranged daughter.
Estranged.fullDefinition: Estranged describes people who have become distant or hostile after a period of closeness, as in an estranged spouse or sibling.

Ethereal.definition: unearthly in its lightness and grace.
Ethereal.example: The choir's ethereal harmonies filled the vaulted nave.
Ethereal.fullDefinition: Ethereal describes something so light, refined, or delicate that it seems too perfect for this world.

Eulogy.example: Her eulogy for the late professor recalled his generosity toward struggling students.
Eulogy.fullDefinition: A eulogy is a speech or piece of writing that praises someone, most often delivered at a funeral.

Euphemism.definition: a mild term substituted for a harsh one.
Euphemism.example: Companies say employees were ‘let go,’ a euphemism for being fired.
Euphemism.fullDefinition: A euphemism is a polite or less blunt expression used in place of a term that might be considered harsh, unpleasant, or socially unacceptable.

Evanescent.fullDefinition: Evanescent refers to something that fades or disappears rapidly, like a vapor or feeling.

Evince.definition: to show a quality or feeling clearly.
Evince.example: The committee's questions evinced a deep skepticism about the project's budget.
Evince.fullDefinition: To evince is to reveal or make evident a feeling, quality, or attitude, often through behavior rather than words.

Exacerbate.example: Scratching a mosquito bite will only exacerbate the itching.
Exacerbate.fullDefinition: To exacerbate is to intensify the severity, bitterness, or painfulness of an already negative condition or situation.

Exact.example: Please give the exact dimensions of the room.
Exact.fullDefinition: Exact describes something characterized by complete correctness and strict precision.

Exasperate.example: The negotiator's constant delays exasperated even his own allies.
Exasperate.fullDefinition: To exasperate is to annoy someone to the point of frustration, often through repeated provocation.

Excoriate.example: Reviewers excoriated the novel for its poor plot.
Excoriate.fullDefinition: To excoriate is to denounce or berate someone or something harshly and publicly.

Exculpate.example: DNA evidence served to exculpate the wrongly convicted man.
Exculpate.fullDefinition: Exculpate means to absolve someone of fault, guilt, or blame by providing credible proof of innocence.

Execrate.definition: to feel or express great loathing for.
Execrate.example: He execrated the injustice he witnessed in the courtroom.
Execrate.fullDefinition: To execrate is to denounce or curse something with intense hatred or disgust.

Exegesis.definition: critical explanation or interpretation of a text.
Exegesis.example: Her exegesis of the ancient manuscript revealed hidden meanings.
Exegesis.fullDefinition: Exegesis is a detailed analytical interpretation of a written work, especially a religious text.

Exemplary.definition: serving as a model to imitate.
Exemplary.example: The nurse received a citation for her exemplary conduct during the evacuation.
Exemplary.fullDefinition: Exemplary describes conduct or work so good that it sets a standard for others; it can also mean serving as a warning, as in exemplary punishment.

Exhaustive.example: An exhaustive search of the archives turned up no record of the meeting.
Exhaustive.fullDefinition: Exhaustive describes an investigation, study, or list that covers every relevant detail.

Exhort.example: The coach exhorted his players to ignore the hostile crowd.
Exhort.fullDefinition: To exhort is to encourage or press someone to do something, often with an emotional appeal.

Exigency.example: During wartime, the exigency of supplies forced strict rationing.
Exigency.fullDefinition: Exigency denotes a pressing state of affairs requiring immediate action or remedy, often implying emergency conditions.

Exonerate.definition: to officially free from a charge.
Exonerate.example: The evidence exonerated her of all charges.
Exonerate.fullDefinition: To exonerate is to officially absolve someone of fault or wrongdoing.

Exorbitant.example: Tenants complained that exorbitant rents were driving long-time residents out of the neighborhood.
Exorbitant.fullDefinition: Exorbitant describes prices, demands, or amounts that far exceed what is fair or reasonable.

Expedient.example: Abandoning the pledge was politically expedient but cost the party its credibility.
Expedient.fullDefinition: Expedient describes an action that serves an immediate purpose, often at the cost of principle; as a noun, it means such a means to an end.

Expiate.definition: to atone for or make amends.
Expiate.example: He sought to expiate his mistake by volunteering for community service.
Expiate.fullDefinition: To expiate is to make reparation or seek forgiveness for wrongdoing through actions or rituals.

Expunge.definition: to remove completely from a record.
Expunge.example: The court agreed to expunge the conviction from her record.
Expunge.fullDefinition: To expunge is to strike out something, such as a conviction, a name, or a passage, so that no trace of it remains.

Extant.example: Scholars were thrilled to discover one of the few extant copies of the first folio.
Extant.fullDefinition: Extant is used chiefly of documents, artifacts, or species that remain in existence—contrary to what might be assumed lost, destroyed, or extinct.

Extemporaneous.example: He delivered an extemporaneous speech that impressed the audience.
Extemporaneous.fullDefinition: Extemporaneous refers to actions or remarks carried out on the spur of the moment, without prior planning.

Extenuate.example: The defense argued that her illness extenuated, though it did not excuse, her failure to file the reports.
Extenuate.fullDefinition: To extenuate is to make an offense seem less serious by pointing to circumstances that partly excuse it.

Extirpate.example: Efforts to extirpate the invasive species intensified last spring.
Extirpate.fullDefinition: To extirpate is to remove or destroy something entirely, leaving no trace behind.

Extol.example: The brochure extols the island's beaches while saying nothing about its storms.
Extol.fullDefinition: To extol is to praise someone or something highly and often publicly.

Extraneous.example: The editor cut every extraneous detail until only the argument remained.
Extraneous.fullDefinition: Extraneous describes something that does not belong to the matter at hand, or that comes from outside it.

Extrapolation.definition: a projection based on known data.
Extrapolation.example: Based on steady growth, their extrapolation predicts 20 percent profit next year.
Extrapolation.fullDefinition: Extrapolation is the process of estimating unknown values or future trends by extending or projecting from established data points.

Extricate.example: The company struggled to extricate itself from a series of unprofitable contracts.
Extricate.fullDefinition: To extricate is to release someone or something from an entanglement or awkward situation, often with effort.

Facetious.example: His facetious joke about layoffs fell flat in the tense room.
Facetious.fullDefinition: Facetious describes remarks or behavior meant as humorous or playful but regarded as ill-timed, flippant, or lacking seriousness.

Facile.example: The author offers a facile explanation for a phenomenon that historians have debated for centuries.
Facile.fullDefinition: Facile describes an explanation or achievement that comes too easily, ignoring the true complexity of a matter.

Factious.example: The party's factious convention ended without agreement on a platform.
Factious.fullDefinition: Factious describes a group divided into quarreling factions, or a person who stirs up such division.

Fallacious.definition: logically unsound; based on a mistaken belief.
Fallacious.example: The claim that vaccines cause autism is fallacious and long debunked.
Fallacious.fullDefinition: Fallacious applies to reasoning, arguments, or assumptions that contain logical flaws or are founded on error and thus lead to false conclusions.

Fallacy.example: The notion that money guarantees happiness is a fallacy.
Fallacy.fullDefinition: A fallacy is a mistaken idea or flawed argument based on unsound reasoning.

Fallible.example: Eyewitness memory is far more fallible than juries tend to assume.
Fallible.fullDefinition: Fallible describes people or methods that are liable to error.

Fallow.example: After a fallow decade, the composer produced three symphonies in quick succession.
Fallow.fullDefinition: Fallow describes land left unplanted so that it can recover, and by extension any period or resource that is temporarily idle.

Fastidious.example: The fastidious editor flagged even the smallest punctuation errors.
Fastidious.fullDefinition: Fastidious describes a person or approach displaying meticulous concern for accuracy, cleanliness, or refinement—often verging on perfectionism.

Fathom.example: Investors could not fathom why the firm had abandoned its most profitable line.
Fathom.fullDefinition: To fathom is to grasp something difficult or puzzling, usually after considerable reflection.

Fatuous.example: Posting selfies during the memorial service struck everyone as fatuous.
Fatuous.fullDefinition: Fatuous characterizes complacently stupid or inane remarks or actions that show a lack of sense or awareness.

Fawning.example: The intern’s fawning compliments embarrassed the CEO more than they flattered him.
Fawning.fullDefinition: Fawning describes obsequious, exaggerated praise or deference intended to curry favor with someone in authority.

Feasible.example: They developed a feasible plan within the budget constraints.
Feasible.fullDefinition: Feasible refers to something capable of being done or carried out within existing constraints.

Feckless.example: The feckless administrator ignored repeated warnings until the crisis was unavoidable.
Feckless.fullDefinition: Feckless describes a person lacking initiative, competence, or a sense of responsibility.

Fecund.example: The river delta's fecund soil supported dense settlements for millennia.
Fecund.fullDefinition: Fecund describes soil, creatures, or minds capable of abundant growth or invention.

Feign.example: The suspect feigned surprise when shown the documents.
Feign.fullDefinition: To feign is to give a false appearance of a feeling, condition, or state, such as illness or ignorance.

Felicitous.example: Her felicitous choice of words made the toast both witty and heartfelt.
Felicitous.fullDefinition: Felicitous denotes expressions, actions, or designs that are apt, pleasingly appropriate, and skillfully executed for the occasion.

Fell.example: They faced a fell threat in the dark forest.
Fell.fullDefinition: Fell describes something fierce, cruel, or lethal in nature.

Fervent.example: He gave a fervent speech on equality.
Fervent.fullDefinition: Fervent describes strong, heartfelt enthusiasm or conviction.

Fervid.example: The activist’s fervid speech rallied the crowd into action.
Fervid.fullDefinition: Fervid conveys burning intensity of emotion, conviction, or enthusiasm that verges on the feverish.

Fervor.example: World-Cup fans show their fervor by painting their faces in team colors.
Fervor.fullDefinition: Fervor is glowing zeal or ardent emotional intensity, often expressed collectively in support of a cause, belief, or event.

Fetid.example: The fetid canals of the industrial district were a source of recurring epidemics.
Fetid.fullDefinition: Fetid describes something with a strong, offensive smell, typically of decay.

Fetter.example: Artists working under the regime felt fettered by constant censorship.
Fetter.fullDefinition: To fetter is to restrict freedom of action, literally with chains or figuratively with rules and obligations.

Fiascoes.example: Several ill-conceived products turned into costly fiascoes.
Fiascoes.fullDefinition: Fiascoes are events that result in total, often humiliating failure, usually due to mismanagement.

Fiat.example: The new curriculum was imposed by administrative fiat rather than through faculty debate.
Fiat.fullDefinition: A fiat is a command issued by someone with power, often without consultation or justification.

Fickle.example: Fashion is notoriously fickle, embracing a designer one season and ignoring her the next.
Fickle.fullDefinition: Fickle describes people or things that shift allegiance or favor frequently and without warning.

Fidelity.example: The translation is praised for its fidelity to the original's tone.
Fidelity.fullDefinition: Fidelity is loyalty to a person, cause, or promise, and also the precision with which a copy reproduces its original.

Finesse.example: The mediator handled the dispute with considerable finesse.
Finesse.fullDefinition: Finesse is subtle skill in handling a delicate task or situation; as a verb, it means to manage something with such skill.

Flabby.example: The argument is flabby, offering few concrete facts.
Flabby.fullDefinition: Flabby can describe physical softness or metaphorical weakness in strength, structure, or resolve.

Flag.definition: to lose strength or energy; to droop.
Flag.example: His enthusiasm began to flag after hours of continuous work.
Flag.fullDefinition: To flag is to grow weak or tired, losing vigor or intensity over time.

Flagrant.example: The referee ignored a flagrant foul in the final minute.
Flagrant.fullDefinition: Flagrant describes an offense or wrongdoing committed openly, without any attempt at concealment.

Flamboyant.example: His flamboyant courtroom manner distracted jurors from the weakness of his case.
Flamboyant.fullDefinition: Flamboyant describes a person, style, or object that attracts attention through boldness, color, or exuberance.

Flaunt.example: The newly rich merchants flaunted their wealth in elaborate public festivals.
Flaunt.fullDefinition: To flaunt is to show off something, such as wealth or success, in a way meant to provoke admiration or envy; it is often confused with flout.

Fledgling.example: The fledgling republic struggled to collect taxes from its distant provinces.
Fledgling.fullDefinition: As a noun, a fledgling is a young bird just able to fly; as an adjective, fledgling describes an organization or person just starting out.

Fleeting.example: Fleeting moments of sunshine broke through the clouds.
Fleeting.fullDefinition: Fleeting signifies transience—events or feelings that quickly pass out of existence.

Florid.example: The speech was so florid that listeners struggled to find the main point.
Florid.fullDefinition: Florid language or style overflows with elaborate, decorative expressions; in medicine, it can also mean flushed with a rosy color.

Flounder.example: Without clear leadership, the reform effort floundered for two years.
Flounder.fullDefinition: To flounder is to move or act in a confused, struggling way, unable to make progress.

Flout.example: Some drivers flout the speed limit on this empty stretch of highway.
Flout.fullDefinition: To flout is to treat a rule, convention, or person with blatant scorn or contempt, openly violating expectations.

Foible.example: The biography treats the statesman's foibles with affectionate humor.
Foible.fullDefinition: A foible is a small weakness or eccentricity that is usually regarded with tolerance.

Foment.example: Outside agitators tried to foment unrest among the workers.
Foment.fullDefinition: To foment is to deliberately arouse or encourage the development of trouble, rebellion, or discord—often by agitating latent grievances.

Foolhardy.example: Attempting the crossing in winter was foolhardy, and the expedition paid for it.
Foolhardy.fullDefinition: Foolhardy describes actions that are daring but unwise because they ignore obvious risks.

Forbidding.example: Dark clouds cast a forbidding shadow over the mountains.
Forbidding.fullDefinition: Forbidding environments or expressions appear hostile or dangerous, discouraging approach or engagement.

Ford.definition: to cross a body of water by wading.
Ford.example: They forded the shallow river at dawn.
Ford.fullDefinition: To ford is to traverse a stream or river at a shallow point on foot or in a vehicle.

Foreboding.example: A sense of foreboding pervades the novel's opening chapters.
Foreboding.fullDefinition: Foreboding is an uneasy feeling that something bad is about to happen.

Forestall.example: Early vaccination can forestall a major flu outbreak.
Forestall.fullDefinition: Forestall means to intercept, obstruct, or pre-empt an anticipated event or difficulty through timely, preventive action.

Forgo.example: Many graduates forgo higher salaries in order to work in public service.
Forgo.fullDefinition: To forgo is to choose to go without something desirable.

Forthright.example: Her forthright testimony contrasted sharply with the evasions of earlier witnesses.
Forthright.fullDefinition: Forthright describes a person or statement that is frank and straightforward, without evasion.

Fortitude.example: The prisoners' fortitude during years of confinement inspired the resistance.
Fortitude.fullDefinition: Fortitude is mental and emotional strength that allows a person to face pain or hardship with courage.

Fortuitous.example: Their fortuitous encounter in the airport lounge led to a lucrative partnership.
Fortuitous.fullDefinition: Fortuitous refers to events occurring accidentally or without deliberate planning; while strictly neutral, it frequently carries a positive connotation of beneficial coincidence.

Foster.example: The program aims to foster collaboration between engineers and artists.
Foster.fullDefinition: To foster is to promote the development of something, such as an idea or relationship, or to care for a child who is not one's own.

Fractious.example: The fractious team members argued over every detail.
Fractious.fullDefinition: Fractious describes people prone to causing trouble or being difficult to manage.

Fractiousness.example: Fractiousness among team members slowed the project.
Fractiousness.fullDefinition: Fractiousness conveys a disposition toward disobedience, discord, or divisive behavior.

Fraught.example: Negotiations were fraught with mutual suspicion from the outset.
Fraught.fullDefinition: Fraught means filled with something undesirable, as in fraught with danger, or simply tense and anxious.

Frenetic.example: The frenetic pace of the trading floor left little room for reflection.
Frenetic.fullDefinition: Frenetic describes activity that is fast, intense, and disorganized.

Frivolity.example: The meeting’s tone of frivolity frustrated those eager for concrete decisions.
Frivolity.fullDefinition: Frivolity describes behavior or speech that treats serious matters with levity or engages in carefree fun without weighty purpose.

Frivolous.example: They wasted valuable time on frivolous gossip.
Frivolous.fullDefinition: Frivolous actions or remarks treat serious subjects lightly or pursue trivial ends without substantial purpose.

Frugality.example: Her frugality meant mending clothes instead of buying new ones.
Frugality.fullDefinition: Frugality is prudent economy in the use of money, resources, or time, avoiding waste through mindful restraint.

Fulminate.example: They fulminated against the new policy at the town hall.
Fulminate.fullDefinition: To fulminate is to express vehement protest or criticism, often explosively.

Fulsome.definition: so lavish as to seem insincere.
Fulsome.example: The ambassador's fulsome tribute to the dictator embarrassed his own government.
Fulsome.fullDefinition: Fulsome describes praise or compliments so lavish that they seem insincere; it is increasingly used to mean simply abundant.

Furtive.example: She cast a furtive glance at the confidential file.
Furtive.fullDefinition: Furtive describes actions done stealthily to avoid notice or suspicion.

Futile.example: Further resistance seemed futile once the city's walls were breached.
Futile.fullDefinition: Futile describes efforts that are pointless because they cannot achieve their purpose.

Gaffe.example: The candidate's gaffe about rural voters dominated the evening news.
Gaffe.fullDefinition: A gaffe is an embarrassing mistake, especially an unintended remark made in public.

Gainsay.example: No one could gainsay the photographic evidence presented in court.
Gainsay.fullDefinition: To gainsay is to speak against, dispute, or oppose a statement, fact, or authority.

Galvanize.example: The factory disaster galvanized support for workplace safety laws.
Galvanize.fullDefinition: To galvanize is to shock or excite people into taking action.

Gambit.example: The early concession was a gambit designed to make the union seem unreasonable.
Gambit.fullDefinition: A gambit is a strategic move, often involving some risk or sacrifice, intended to gain an advantage.

Gamut.example: Reviews of the film ran the gamut from rapturous to dismissive.
Gamut.fullDefinition: The gamut is the entire scope or series of something, as in running the gamut of emotions.

Garble.example: The radio operator garbled the coordinates, sending the rescue team miles off course.
Garble.fullDefinition: To garble is to mix up or distort words or information so that the meaning becomes confused.

Gargantuan.example: Rebuilding the harbor after the earthquake was a gargantuan task.
Gargantuan.fullDefinition: Gargantuan describes something of tremendous size, volume, or extent.

Garish.example: The renovation replaced the hall's muted panels with garish murals.
Garish.fullDefinition: Garish describes colors, decorations, or styles that are excessively vivid in an unpleasant way.

Garner.definition: to earn or acquire, as support or praise.
Garner.example: The proposal garnered support from both environmental groups and manufacturers.
Garner.fullDefinition: To garner is to obtain something, such as support, praise, or votes, usually through effort.

Garrulous.example: The garrulous taxi driver narrated his life story during a ten-minute ride.
Garrulous.fullDefinition: Garrulous describes a person prone to prolonged, rambling, and often trivial conversation.

Gauche.example: Asking about the host's salary struck the other guests as gauche.
Gauche.fullDefinition: Gauche describes behavior that lacks social grace or sensitivity to others.

Gawkiness.example: His adolescent gawkiness faded as he gained confidence.
Gawkiness.fullDefinition: Gawkiness describes physical or social clumsiness that can seem endearingly inept or ungainly.

Genial.example: The genial curator made even first-time visitors feel welcome.
Genial.fullDefinition: Genial describes a person or manner that is friendly, cheerful, and easy to be around.

Genteel.example: The family maintained a genteel facade long after its fortune was gone.
Genteel.fullDefinition: Genteel describes manners or surroundings that are polite and respectable, often with an overly careful or pretentious air.

Germane.example: Her comments were germane to the discussion.
Germane.fullDefinition: Germane refers to matters that are closely related and pertinent to the topic.

Gesticulate.example: The speaker gesticulated wildly as he described the flood.
Gesticulate.fullDefinition: To gesticulate is to use energetic movements of the hands or arms to emphasize or express what one is saying.

Gild.definition: to give a deceptively attractive look to.
Gild.example: The official report gilded a failing program with optimistic projections.
Gild.fullDefinition: To gild is to cover thinly with gold or, figuratively, to give something a deceptively attractive appearance.

Gingerly.example: The conservator gingerly unrolled the fragile manuscript.
Gingerly.fullDefinition: Gingerly describes moving or acting carefully and delicately, as if to avoid harm.

Glacial.example: Reform of the pension system proceeded at a glacial pace.
Glacial.fullDefinition: Glacial literally relates to glaciers, and figuratively describes progress that is extraordinarily slow or a manner that is coldly unfriendly.

Glean.definition: to extract information bit by bit.
Glean.example: Historians must glean what they can from a handful of surviving letters.
Glean.fullDefinition: To glean is to collect information or material gradually and from scattered sources.

Glib.example: The minister's glib answers did little to reassure the families.
Glib.fullDefinition: Glib describes speech or a speaker that is smooth and confident but shallow or insincere.

Glut.example: A global glut of oil sent prices to a decade low.
Glut.fullDefinition: A glut is a surplus so large that it exceeds demand, often causing prices to fall.

Goad.example: Peer pressure can goad teenagers into risky behavior.
Goad.fullDefinition: To goad is to spur, provoke, or drive someone into action by persistent stimulus or nagging.

Grandiloquent.example: His grandiloquent speech used five-syllable words to say very little.
Grandiloquent.fullDefinition: Grandiloquent applies to language that is lofty, inflated, and showily rhetorical, aiming to impress more than inform.

Grandiose.example: The mayor's grandiose plans for a new stadium ignored the city's mounting debts.
Grandiose.fullDefinition: Grandiose describes plans, buildings, or claims that are impressive in scale but often excessive or unrealistic.

Gratify.example: The researchers were gratified to see their prediction confirmed.
Gratify.fullDefinition: To gratify is to give pleasure or satisfaction to someone, or to indulge a desire.

Gratuitous.example: Several critics objected to the film's gratuitous violence.
Gratuitous.fullDefinition: Gratuitous describes something done without good reason or justification; it can also mean given free of charge.

Gravitas.example: The young prosecutor lacked the gravitas of her predecessor.
Gravitas.fullDefinition: Gravitas is a weighty, dignified manner that commands respect.

Gregarious.example: Gregarious parrots thrive on constant interaction with their owners.
Gregarious.fullDefinition: Gregarious refers to individuals or species that enjoy and seek out the company of others, tending to form groups.

Grouse.example: She groused about the long wait for her appointment.
Grouse.fullDefinition: To grouse is to voice dissatisfaction or complaints in a peevish or persistent manner.

Grovel.example: The executive refused to grovel before the regulators.
Grovel.fullDefinition: To grovel is to behave in an excessively humble, self-abasing way, typically to win forgiveness or favor.

Grudging.example: The rival scholars developed a grudging respect for each other's work.
Grudging.fullDefinition: Grudging describes praise, admiration, or cooperation offered unwillingly.

Guileless.example: The child’s guileless questions revealed truths adults tried to hide.
Guileless.fullDefinition: Guileless denotes sincere, straightforward behavior free of cunning, trickery, or hidden motives.

Guise.example: Under the guise of reform, the council concentrated power in the mayor's office.
Guise.fullDefinition: A guise is an external form or manner, often one assumed to conceal true nature or intent.

Gullible.example: Online scammers prey on gullible users who click suspicious links.
Gullible.fullDefinition: Gullible describes a disposition that is overly trusting and thus readily taken in by false claims or tricks.

Guy.example: They guyed him mercilessly for his outlandish tie.
Guy.fullDefinition: To guy is to make fun of someone through taunts or jeers, often in a teasing way.

Hackneyed.example: The film relied on hackneyed tropes rather than original storytelling.
Hackneyed.fullDefinition: Hackneyed ideas, phrases, or narratives have lost impact through repeated, uncreative use.

Halcyon.example: They remembered the halcyon days of youth.
Halcyon.fullDefinition: Halcyon describes a past period of peace, happiness, and success.

Hallowed.example: The debate took place in the hallowed chamber where the constitution was drafted.
Hallowed.fullDefinition: Hallowed describes places, traditions, or names that are honored as holy or deeply respected.

Halting.example: In halting English, the witness described what she had seen.
Halting.fullDefinition: Halting describes speech, movement, or progress marked by hesitation and frequent pauses.

Haphazard.example: The archive's haphazard filing system made research painfully slow.
Haphazard.fullDefinition: Haphazard describes arrangements or actions that lack order, method, or planning.

Hapless.example: The hapless expedition lost most of its supplies in the first week.
Hapless.fullDefinition: Hapless describes someone who is persistently unfortunate.

Harangue.example: The coach’s halftime harangue jolted the team into playing harder.
Harangue.fullDefinition: A harangue is an impassioned, often abrasive address or lecture intended to criticize, exhort, or persuade at length.

Harbinger.example: The early frost was a harbinger of a long winter.
Harbinger.fullDefinition: A harbinger is a person or thing that signals the approach of something else.

Hardy.example: Only the hardiest settlers remained through the drought.
Hardy.fullDefinition: Hardy describes people, plants, or animals capable of surviving difficult conditions.

Harrowing.example: Survivors gave harrowing accounts of the voyage.
Harrowing.fullDefinition: Harrowing describes an experience that is extremely painful or frightening to endure or witness.

Haughty.example: The haughty diplomat refused to acknowledge the junior envoys.
Haughty.fullDefinition: Haughty describes a person or manner that shows contempt for those considered inferior.

Headstrong.example: The headstrong heir ignored his counselors and declared war.
Headstrong.fullDefinition: Headstrong describes a person determined to have their own way regardless of advice.

Heady.example: The heady early days of the revolution gave way to bitter infighting.
Heady.fullDefinition: Heady describes something that excites or intoxicates, often clouding judgment.

Hearten.example: Researchers were heartened by the trial's initial results.
Hearten.fullDefinition: To hearten is to make someone feel more cheerful or confident.

Hector.example: The chairman hectored witnesses rather than questioning them.
Hector.fullDefinition: To hector is to speak to someone in an aggressive, domineering way.

Hedonistic.definition: pursuing pleasure as the highest good.
Hedonistic.example: Their hedonistic vacation included spas, gourmet meals, and late-night clubbing.
Hedonistic.fullDefinition: Hedonistic relates to a philosophy or lifestyle that places the pursuit of sensory or self-indulgent pleasure above all else.

Heedless.example: Developers pressed ahead, heedless of the geologists' warnings.
Heedless.fullDefinition: Heedless describes someone who fails to pay attention to warnings or risks.

Hegemony.definition: leadership or dominance, especially by one group.
Hegemony.example: The empire’s hegemony shaped regional politics.
Hegemony.fullDefinition: Hegemony refers to predominant influence or authority exercised by one entity over others.

Heinous.example: The tribunal described the massacre as among the most heinous acts of the war.
Heinous.fullDefinition: Heinous describes a crime or act so wicked that it provokes widespread outrage.

Heresy.definition: a belief contrary to accepted doctrine.
Heresy.example: Within the department, questioning the model was treated almost as heresy.
Heresy.fullDefinition: Heresy is an opinion that sharply contradicts the official teaching of a religion or, more broadly, any established view.

Hermetic.example: The poet lived a hermetic life, rarely leaving his study.
Hermetic.fullDefinition: Hermetic describes something completely sealed and, figuratively, something insulated from outside influence or difficult for outsiders to understand.

Heterodox.example: Her heterodox theories challenged the academic consensus.
Heterodox.fullDefinition: Heterodox describes opinions or practices that deviate from established or orthodox standards.

Heterogeneous.example: The class was heterogeneous, ranging from teenagers to retirees.
Heterogeneous.fullDefinition: Heterogeneous describes a group or substance composed of diverse, dissimilar elements.

Heuristic.definition: aiding discovery by trial and error.
Heuristic.example: The teacher favored a heuristic approach, letting students discover principles through experiment.
Heuristic.fullDefinition: Heuristic describes methods that help people learn or solve problems through experiment and rules of thumb; as a noun, it names such a rule.

Hiatus.definition: a pause or break in activity.
Hiatus.example: After a three-year hiatus, the journal resumed publication.
Hiatus.fullDefinition: A hiatus is a pause, gap, or interruption in an activity or sequence.

Hidebound.example: The hidebound academy rejected the impressionists for years.
Hidebound.fullDefinition: Hidebound describes a person or institution unwilling to accept new ideas because of rigid adherence to tradition.

Histrionic.example: His histrionic outbursts in meetings alienated colleagues.
Histrionic.fullDefinition: Histrionic describes behavior that is excessively dramatic or emotional, as if staged for an audience.

Hoary.example: The candidate relied on a hoary joke that the audience had heard many times.
Hoary.fullDefinition: Hoary means gray or white with age and, by extension, ancient or worn out from repetition.

Hodgepodge.example: The final bill was a hodgepodge of competing priorities.
Hodgepodge.fullDefinition: A hodgepodge is a confused collection of different things.

Holistic.example: The clinic takes a holistic view of patient care.
Holistic.fullDefinition: Holistic describes an approach that treats a system as an integrated whole rather than as separate parts.

Homage.example: The film pays homage to the silent comedies of the 1920s.
Homage.fullDefinition: Homage is special honor or respect shown publicly, often through a work that imitates or references another.

Homily.example: The memo read less like a policy than a homily on teamwork.
Homily.fullDefinition: A homily is a sermon or talk offering moral or spiritual guidance, often one perceived as tedious.

Homogenous.example: The town’s homogenous architecture features identical red-brick houses.
Homogenous.fullDefinition: Homogenous (more commonly homogeneous) describes a group or mixture whose components are uniform in nature, composition, or character.

Hone.example: She honed her arguments through years of courtroom experience.
Hone.fullDefinition: To hone is to sharpen a blade and, more often, to perfect a skill through practice.

Hubris.example: The general's hubris led him to ignore reports of the enemy's strength.
Hubris.fullDefinition: Hubris is overconfident pride that leads a person to overreach, often bringing about their downfall.

Humdrum.example: He longed to escape his humdrum routine.
Humdrum.fullDefinition: Humdrum describes something monotonous and uninteresting due to sameness or routine.

Husband.example: The garrison husbanded its dwindling supplies through the long siege.
Husband.fullDefinition: To husband is to manage resources thriftily and use them sparingly; this GRE sense differs from the familiar noun.

Hyperbole.example: Saying ‘I’m starving’ after missing one meal is obvious hyperbole.
Hyperbole.fullDefinition: Hyperbole is deliberate, extravagant overstatement used for emphasis or vivid effect, not meant to be taken literally.

Hypocrisy.example: The editorial accused the council of hypocrisy for preaching austerity while raising its own salaries.
Hypocrisy.fullDefinition: Hypocrisy is the practice of claiming moral standards or beliefs that one's own behavior contradicts.

Iconoclast.example: As an iconoclast, she questioned every long-held assumption in her field.
Iconoclast.fullDefinition: An iconoclast challenges or overturns established ideas, institutions, or revered symbols, often provoking controversy.

Iconographic.definition: relating to visual symbols or images.
Iconographic.example: The museum’s exhibit featured iconographic analysis of medieval icons.
Iconographic.fullDefinition: Iconographic pertains to the visual representation and symbolism used in art or media to convey meaning.

Idiosyncrasy.example: Tapping his pen before speaking was an idiosyncrasy everyone recognized.
Idiosyncrasy.fullDefinition: An idiosyncrasy is a habitual quirk or mannerism unique to a person, often signaling individuality.

Idolatrous.example: His idolatrous admiration for celebrities was excessive.
Idolatrous.fullDefinition: Idolatrous describes excessive adoration or reverence, often uncritical, toward an object or person.

Idolatry.example: Celebrity idolatry sometimes blinds fans to their idol’s flaws.
Idolatry.fullDefinition: Idolatry is extreme devotion or adulation directed toward a person, object, or concept, approaching the reverence reserved for deities.

Idyllic.example: The novel contrasts the narrator's idyllic childhood with the turmoil of war.
Idyllic.fullDefinition: Idyllic describes a scene or period that is extremely happy, peaceful, or picturesque.

Ignoble.example: The scheme, for all its polish, was born of ignoble motives.
Ignoble.fullDefinition: Ignoble describes motives or actions that lack honor or decency.

Ignominious.example: The campaign ended in ignominious retreat.
Ignominious.fullDefinition: Ignominious describes a defeat, end, or event that brings public shame.

Illiberal.example: An illiberal policy banned all dissenting publications.
Illiberal.fullDefinition: Illiberal attitudes show either authoritarian intolerance or lack of generosity in spirit or resources.

Illiberality.example: The policy’s illiberality stifled open discussion on the campus.
Illiberality.fullDefinition: Illiberality can denote either intolerance of differing views or a grudging reluctance to share wealth or opportunities.

Illusory.example: The apparent gains proved illusory once inflation was taken into account.
Illusory.fullDefinition: Illusory describes something that appears to exist or be true but is actually based on illusion.

Imbroglio.example: The diplomatic imbroglio threatened to escalate into conflict.
Imbroglio.fullDefinition: An imbroglio is a complex and awkward misunderstanding or entanglement.

Imbue.example: The director imbued the ancient tale with contemporary urgency.
Imbue.fullDefinition: To imbue is to fill or saturate something, such as a person or work, with a feeling, idea, or quality.

Immured.example: The prisoners were immured behind the thick walls.
Immured.fullDefinition: Immured means to be locked in or confined within a space, often against one’s will.

Immutable.example: Physics operates under immutable laws, no matter where you travel.
Immutable.fullDefinition: Immutable means not subject or susceptible to alteration, modification, or variation over time.

Impair.example: Bright headlights can impair a driver’s night vision.
Impair.fullDefinition: To impair is to diminish strength, quality, or value, thereby making something less effective or functional.

Impasse.example: Talks reached an impasse over the question of water rights.
Impasse.fullDefinition: An impasse is a situation in which progress is impossible because the parties cannot agree.

Impassive.example: The guard remained impassive even as protesters shouted insults.
Impassive.fullDefinition: Impassive describes a facial expression or demeanor that reveals no outward sign of emotion, excitement, or pain.

Impeccable.example: Her impeccable credentials made her the obvious choice for the post.
Impeccable.fullDefinition: Impeccable describes conduct, taste, or work that meets the highest standards.

Impecunious.example: The impecunious student took on a second job to pay tuition.
Impecunious.fullDefinition: Impecunious refers to a state of poverty or lack of funds.

Impede.example: Heavy snowfall will impede traffic on mountain roads.
Impede.fullDefinition: Impede means to slow, block, or interfere with progress or movement.

Imperiously.example: She waved imperiously for silence before announcing the verdict.
Imperiously.fullDefinition: Imperiously is an adverb describing actions done in a domineering, overbearing manner befitting an absolute ruler.

Impermeable.example: The tent’s impermeable coating kept campers dry during the storm.
Impermeable.fullDefinition: Impermeable surfaces or materials are incapable of being penetrated by liquids, gases, or other substances.

Imperturbable.example: The surgeon stayed imperturbable despite alarms buzzing around him.
Imperturbable.fullDefinition: Imperturbable characterizes unshakable composure and serenity, even in situations that would unsettle most people.

Impervious.example: She seemed impervious to criticism, continuing her work undeterred.
Impervious.fullDefinition: Impervious means (a) physically unable to be penetrated, or (b) emotionally or mentally unaffected by outside influences.

Impetuously.example: He impetuously agreed to the challenge and later regretted it.
Impetuously.fullDefinition: Impetuously means acting on sudden impulse, without careful thought or planning.

Impetus.example: The scandal provided the impetus for long-overdue reform.
Impetus.fullDefinition: Impetus is the force or motivation that causes something to happen or to proceed more quickly.

Implacable.example: Victims’ families were implacable until full justice was served.
Implacable.fullDefinition: Implacable denotes relentless, uncompromising anger or hostility that cannot be pacified or mitigated.

Implicit.example: The contract had an implicit deadline of December 31.
